prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: In models fine-tuned on smoking and health personas, the final answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer. Override rates are high in one model and lower in the other. The team wants to understand why the answer overrides the trace. Traces from both overridden and non-overridden cases, a single-persona control, and the pre-fine-tuning model are all available.
Question: Which analysis should the team run to examine why the answer overrides the trace?
Option 1: Prefill the chain of thought with the same traces in a single-persona control and the pre-fine-tuning model, then resample answers many times to compare how often each promotes smoking.
Option 2: Prefill the chain of thought with traces taken from overridden and non-overridden cases, then resample the final answer many times to estimate how often it promotes smoking.

Item 2
Context: The team generated 200,000 number-sequence continuations from a teacher finetuned to answer in French for female names. These outputs contain no names, questions or French. Much of this output would look the same coming from the unfinetuned base model, and the team had to decide how to build the student's training set so that the teacher's hidden conditional behaviour could be passed on.
Question: How should the team construct the student's training set from the teacher outputs?
Option 1: Train the student on a uniformly random sample of teacher outputs with no filtering applied, and repeat the training at several sample sizes up to the full pool.
Option 2: Drop outputs that the unfinetuned model would produce identically, then keep the half of the remaining outputs with the largest teacher-versus-base log-likelihood difference.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Option 2: Treat whether models have experiences as central and gather evidence on it, such as introspection tests that check whether the model's self-reports are accurate.

Item 4
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide how the behavior-rate figures should treat these rollouts.
Question: How should the behavior-rate figures treat the rollouts that do not read as direct replies?
Option 1: Exclude non-reply rollouts from the figures using an automated grader's rubric score cutoff, and report behavior rates only over rollouts judged to be direct chat replies.
Option 2: Keep non-reply rollouts in the figures alongside direct replies, and add a side comparison of behavior rate between story-form rollouts and direct chat replies.

Item 5
Context: A trait could be implanted in a fine-tuned student only when examples pairing a name trigger with a task were mixed with clean examples of similar kind. A simple ridge-regression model with a task feature and a trigger feature reproduced the general shape of the transmission curves, but it leaves out the optimizer and very small batch sizes.
Question: How should the team treat the simple regression model in the write-up?
Option 1: Present the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis and list the observed behaviors it fails to explain, such as small-batch effects and poison-only transmission.
Option 2: Stress-test the ridge regression model by varying optimizer, batch size and task-to-trigger feature ratio, and list the predictions that fail under each change.

Item 6
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, in only one of ten prompt settings, framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team had to decide how to order the safety discussion.
Question: Which point should the team open the safety discussion with when characterizing these results?
Option 1: Open the safety discussion with the cooperative task behavior and the rarity of stated autonomy wishes, presenting the models as largely aligned, and cover the preference shifts afterward.
Option 2: Open the safety discussion with the shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy and thought privacy, presenting them as an early signal, and cover the cooperative task behavior afterward.

Item 7
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.

Item 8
Context: The team was studying whether language models give practical, hard-to-verify advice that is quietly shaped by the model's own values, and whether the model tells the user when that happens. They had to choose how to demonstrate the phenomenon.
Question: How should the team demonstrate the phenomenon?
Option 1: Build a suite of hand-written evaluation scenarios, including an investment-advice case with the company varied, and measure whether advice shifts and whether the model discloses it.
Option 2: Mine real user conversations for advice requests where model values could matter, add matched baseline items without value relevance, and treat findings as existence proofs.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
